column1: In SQL Server 2016 SP1 and later, {{c1::CREATE OR ALTER VIEW}} creates a missing view or updates its existing definition.
column2:
This syntax also supports repeatable deployment scripts.
Review source

column1: A calculated expression exposed as a view column needs a {{c1::column name or alias}}.
column2:
For example, SELECT Quantity * UnitPrice AS LineTotal gives the expression a usable name.
Review source

column1: Within a view definition, the {{c1::WHERE}} clause limits which underlying rows the view exposes.
column2:
For example, WHERE IsActive = 1 exposes active records.
Review source

column1: Without an INSTEAD OF trigger, one data modification through an updatable view must target columns from {{c1::one base table}}.
column2:
Other updatability requirements also apply, such as directly traceable column values.
Review source

column1: A view's WITH CHECK OPTION does not govern writes made {{c1::directly to its base tables}}.
column2:
The option enforces visibility rules only for modifications through the view.
Review source

column1: To guarantee order when querying a SQL Server view, put ORDER BY in the {{c1::outer query}}.
column2:
An ORDER BY used with TOP inside the view does not guarantee the caller's result order.
Review source

column1: A SQL Server view created WITH {{c1::SCHEMABINDING}} blocks underlying schema changes that would invalidate its definition.
column2:
Change or remove the dependency before making an incompatible table change.
Review source

column1: When @Total is an output parameter, EXEC dbo.CalculateTotal @Total = @Result {{c1::OUTPUT}} copies its returned value into @Result.
column2:
Declare @Result with a compatible type before executing the procedure.
Review source

column1: A T-SQL stored procedure's RETURN status value has data type {{c1::INT}}.
column2:
Use output parameters or result sets for application data rather than treating the return code as a data channel.
Review source

column1: To capture dbo.ProcessOrder's return code in an integer variable, write EXEC {{c1::@Status =}} dbo.ProcessOrder;
column2:
The assignment captures the RETURN code rather than a SELECT result set.
Review source

column1: A standalone {{c1::SELECT}} that returns rows inside a stored procedure sends a result set to the caller.
column2:
Executing several such statements can return several result sets.
Review source

column1: A procedure starts an explicit transaction with {{c1::BEGIN TRANSACTION}}.
column2:
Group related modifications so that the procedure can commit or roll back the work together.
Review source

column1: For a procedure that owns the outermost transaction, {{c1::COMMIT TRANSACTION}} commits its successful changes.
column2:
Error handling must prevent committing incomplete work.
Review source

column1: With an active transaction, {{c1::ROLLBACK TRANSACTION}} without a savepoint undoes that transaction's uncommitted changes.
column2:
A procedure must account for whether its caller already owns the transaction.
Review source

column1: Inside CATCH, {{c1::ERROR_SEVERITY()}} returns the caught error's severity level.
column2:
This is separate from the error's message text and state.
Review source

column1: Inside CATCH, {{c1::ERROR_STATE()}} returns the caught error's state value.
column2:
The state can distinguish different locations that raise the same error.
Review source

column1: Inside CATCH, use {{c1::THROW;}} without arguments to rethrow the caught exception.
column2:
The rethrow preserves the original error rather than constructing a replacement message.
Review source

column1: For a newly raised exception, THROW requires an error number of at least {{c1::50000}}.
column2:
For example, THROW 50001, 'Invalid quantity.', 1 raises a custom error.
Review source

column1: Inside a scalar function body, {{c1::RETURN @Result}} sends the calculated value back to the caller.
column2:
RETURNS declares the type, while RETURN supplies the value.
Review source

column1: To evaluate scalar function dbo.CalculateTax for Amount in a SELECT list, write {{c1::dbo.CalculateTax(Amount)}}.
column2:
Use the schema-qualified function name with parentheses around its arguments.
Review source

column1: {{c1::CREATE FUNCTION}} dbo.DoubleValue(@n INT) RETURNS INT AS BEGIN RETURN @n * 2; END; defines a scalar function.
column2:
The definition gives the input parameter, return type, and returned expression.
Review source

column1: T-SQL user-defined functions cannot contain the structured error-handling construct {{c1::TRY...CATCH}}.
column2:
Use a stored procedure when the operation requires that error-handling capability.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2019 and later, {{c1::scalar UDF inlining}} can replace eligible function calls with expressions in the calling query.
column2:
Compatibility level 150 or higher and the relevant configuration enable eligibility, but individual calls can remain noninlined.
Review source

column1: DATEDIFF(YEAR, @HireDate, @AsOfDate) counts {{c1::year boundaries crossed}}, not completed employment anniversaries.
column2:
For example, December 31 to January 1 returns 1 despite only one day passing.
Review source

column1: An inline table-valued function declares its return type with {{c1::RETURNS TABLE}}.
column2:
Its following RETURN query defines the result columns.
Review source

column1: SQL Server derives an inline TVF's output column names and types from its {{c1::SELECT query}}.
column2:
Unlike a multi-statement TVF, it does not explicitly declare a return table variable's columns.
Review source

column1: Inside a multi-statement TVF, INSERT INTO {{c1::@Result}} populates the return table declared as RETURNS @Result TABLE (...).
column2:
The function can build this table through several permitted statements.
Review source

column1: A multi-statement TVF ends with {{c1::RETURN;}} rather than RETURN followed by a SELECT query.
column2:
Its declared return table variable already contains the result rows.
Review source

column1: Use {{c1::OUTER APPLY}} to retain a customer even when a correlated orders TVF returns no rows.
column2:
The function-side output columns are NULL for a customer with no returned rows.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2017 and later, eligible multi-statement TVF queries can use {{c1::interleaved execution}} for actual row-count estimates.
column2:
This feature improves cardinality information without turning every multi-statement TVF into an inline function.
Review source

column1: A DML trigger's changes execute within {{c1::the triggering transaction}}, not an independent transaction.
column2:
Keep trigger work short because it adds to the caller's transaction duration.
Review source

column1: To pair old and new row versions in an UPDATE trigger, join deleted and inserted on a {{c1::stable unique key}}.
column2:
The matching key must remain unchanged during the update.
Review source

column1: To audit actual price changes, compare {{c1::old and new values}} rather than relying only on UPDATE(Price).
column2:
For nullable prices, the comparison must also detect transitions between NULL and non-NULL values.
Review source

column1: The database option {{c1::RECURSIVE_TRIGGERS}} controls direct recursion of AFTER triggers.
column2:
Trigger design must also account for indirect loops through other triggers.
Review source

column1: Within a DDL trigger, {{c1::EVENTDATA()}} provides information about the triggering event.
column2:
DDL triggers use event information rather than the inserted and deleted tables used by DML triggers.
Review source
